en: And in eighty places
Had them set as lamps.
“Lest the inside rot,” she thought;
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
Showing her lion’s courage,
Had a way broken through with iron crowbars,
Showing her skill,
The dark spring water flowing above
She had led through the interior.
She had a golden couch built,
And covered it with fine white cloth.
“Lest the underside rot,” she thought,
She had juniper ashes spread.
Without letting one person know,
Without letting a single soul suspect,
Without showing the six villains,
Without making it known to the people,
She tended Manas.
If anyone knew a hint of it,
Your sister-in-law deceived and killed them.
For Manas lying ill,
She carefully prepared his belongings;
The dead warrior had not the smallest regret left.
Then fierce Kanykei
Joined what had been broken,
Gathered what had been scattered,
And did not cease her tears.
Precious coins of yellow gold
She gathered for his funeral.
The Muslims of the Islamic faith
Wept in sorrow.
The reason for their weeping:
The leopard was the pillar of the faith.
When they girded themselves, that dear lion—
Was not Manas their backbone?
When they met a task in dire distress,
Without leaving them in ruin,
Was it not Manas who cared for them?
Leaving no part of the earth untouched,
Was it not Manas who ranged across it?
His wrath struck terror into souls;
At the head of the mighty people,
Was it not Manas who stood?
The Chinese upon the ridges—
Was it not Manas who slew them?
All that he did before Allah—
Was it not Manas who won His favor?
The Argyn and the Kyrgyz,
Letting no wind break through from any side,
Was it not Manas who sheltered them?
His fortune was complete;
His heart was a boundless river and lake.
He was a lion upheld by his patron saint.
Yielding to none in all the world,
The lion Manas was a hero.
A grievous sickness came upon him;
Your fierce wolf put them through such trials.
His whiskered mustache drooping,
Setting out toward Judgment Day,
Now his illness grew severe.
As Manas lay upon his pillow,
And fierce Kanykei bore the hardship alone,
She sent word to the khan.
A day of terrible trouble came
For all the people.
Word was sent
To Khan Karacha’s city.
Urging Kartkurong to his dancing stride,
Traversing many a road between,
Traveling far, sparing no horseflesh,
Taking no rest by day,
Taking no sleep at night,
Letting Kartkurong no time to graze,
Never lying on his side to sleep his fill,
Never resting upon his elbow,
Never taking even a brief nap,
To Karacha’s daughter Saikal
Khan Ajybai came.
Khan Ajybai’s arrival
The thousand men posted to watch for news
Saw from the mountainside.
To Karacha’s daughter Saikal
They sent urgent word.
When she heard this news,
Furiously from her palace
The khan of the Oigut came forth.
That scowling, dark Sart,
Ajybai, had arrived—
Your dear Saikal heard.
Hearing it, unable to hold still,
Her splendid hair as thick as a girth
She bound tight upon her crown.
Her iron shield, proof against bullets,
She pressed down upon her head.
The golden-cheeked battle-axe
That took men’s souls,
In the venom of a dragon
Tempered six separate times,
That glowed red when swung,
When it entered the fighting foe
Grew to the length of a rope—
That golden-cheeked battle-axe
She fastened snugly to her wrist.
Drawing it from its sheath with a shout,
She took her sword in hand.
Khan Saikal, Karacha’s daughter,
Struck once more by God’s affliction,
Flew into fury.
No soul could withstand her wrath;
Fire poured from her mouth.
Karacha’s daughter Saikal
Loomed like Mount Opol,
Troubling the hearts of those who saw her.
Karacha’s daughter Saikal—
Her right shoulder was broad.
Were it not for the fault of being female,
She was a warrior who could destroy the world.
Finding no mountain to hurl herself against,
Finding no enemy to fight,
Finding no stone to bite,
Finding no head to sever,
Finding no broad ridge for a camping ground,
Finding no warrior to joust with,
The standard fluttered in her hand;
The painted spear of dark steel
Flashed in her right hand.
Looming like Mount Opol,
Argynkhan’s son Ajybai,
When he saw Khan Saikal,
Was deeply troubled in his heart.
Khan Ajybai, the eloquent slave,
Turned Kartkurong’s head,
Unable to withstand her fury,
He now spoke these words,
How gravely Manas had fallen ill—
He explained the matter to her.
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
Was a woman of sacred power:
“Khan Manas has fallen ill.
‘I shall perform his rites for forty days’—
That was the promise you made.
The leopard lies sick,
That soul of sacred power;
His fine mustache has drooped,
Grave trouble has fallen on him.
‘Let her agree to what I say,’ he says,
‘Let her turn her head toward me a little,’ he says.
‘We pledged to help each other in the next world;
The son I leave behind is young—
Let her preside at my funeral rites,’ he says.
‘Let her lead the people and rule the land,
And perform my service herself,’ he says.
‘If Saykal fails to come,
I shall know she is a liar,’ he says.
‘If what is told is true,
Should Saykal fail to come,
When Judgment Day arrives,
I shall make her a black donkey to ride,’ he says.
He said she must come without fail.
Those are the words he entrusted to me.
Dear Saykal, I have discharged my duty:
Those are my generous Manas’s words.”
When Ajybai said this,
Saykal’s anger rose:
“May your daughter be divorced, Ajybai!
Do not twist your words about!
I shall break your back,
I shall kill you,
I shall gouge out one of your eyes!
Sart Ajybai, you mad slave,
Turn your horse’s head and go!
‘Saykal beat me’—
Go tell your Manas that!
Think about it, Ajybai:
From the spur of the winding mountain,
From its jutting headland,
With mighty Manas in the front
And his forty companions at the sides,
When you drew your bows like pouring rain
And charged in all together,
I took my lacquered spear in hand,
And that lion of yours, your champion Manas,
I knocked clean down with my spear.
I routed his forty companions,
And all except Almambet
I captured and bound then.
Not once did I knock Manas down—
I knocked him down six times with my spear!
That whirling fire kindled on the hills—
They are pursuing us fiercely.
Because he struck me once with his spear,
Your empty-boasting Manas
Has come to think of me as his wife!
As though he had slaughtered a two-humped camel
And openly solemnized our marriage,
He has come to think of me as his wife!
Turn your horse’s head and go!
Let him die twice instead of once—
Go tell your Manas that!”
Furious, the maiden Saykal
From upon Kartküröng,
She seized him by the very hem of his coat.
Ajybai, who had come as an intermediary,
Now brought trouble on his own head.
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
Snatched up a white whip with black side-straps
And swung it round,
Striking Argynkhan’s Ajy
With crack after crack.
That revered Sultan Manas
Was dead became clear today;
Blue-maned Khan Ajybai’s
Back was sliced like curd cheese.
That generous Manas, the morning star,
Was sick became clear today.
She tugged out his mustache and flung it away,
She tore out his beard and flung it away.
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
Raged without stopping;
She took a sword in hand.
His precious Manas was not here—
This was the spectacle she made of him.
“May your daughter be divorced, Ajybai!
Turn your horse’s head and go!
‘Saykal made a spectacle of me’—
Go tell your Manas that!
Do not come back a second time
And appear before my eyes!
Do not come near me!
I shall dig your grave deep,
I shall boil up misery for you from far and wide!
I shall strip it off and wear it as booty,
If I please—the coat upon your back!
‘This is what Saykal did’—
Take that answer back to your Manas!”
As for Ajybai and Bakai,
Not even a little bird had struck them;
Let alone a woman, to a champion such as Ajybai,
Not even a black giant had dared come near.
While revered Manas was there,
Ajybai had never suffered anyone’s abuse.
His many sorrows overflowed his breast;
Ajybai’s tears streamed in ten channels.
His beard torn clean away,
His whole mustache plucked out,
The poor man moved off into the distance,
That poor head that had seen ruin;
Grieving without cease,
Tears rolled gleaming from his eyes.
Weeping aloud and wasting with sorrow,
He came singing a lament for Manas,
Ajybai, astonished at this shitty world.
“To the black city Kambyl,
When I was laying siege,
The kaldai and shibe officials—
With crashing blows, I, wretched soul,
